A. Does recent evidence support the size of effect we assume: does this measure raise the share of lung cancer patients who get curative-intent treatment, and by how much?
Measure: Thoracic surgeon reviews every decision not to operate. A thoracic surgeon from the university hospital sits in the county lung meeting every week and gives a second opinion before a stage I-II patient is refused surgery. Counties without their own thoracic surgeon decide about surgery without one today.
effect_summary_en: The English study we already hold (Lau et al. 2013) found resection rates of 20.0% where surgeons were based against 11.6% in peripheral hospitals, but it is observational and the abstract does not give the 14.4% vs 12.0% MDT-attendance figures.
supported_en: Lau et al. (J Thorac Oncol 2013) report that hospitals where surgeons were based resected 20.0% of patients, against 11.6% in peripheral hospitals in England.
not_supported_en: The abstract does not show the 2.4-point gain from surgeon attendance at MDT meetings, and no page shows that such a gain carries over to Finland.

in_use_summary_en: Tyks says lung cancer diagnostics for Varsinais-Suomi are centralised at its lung clinic, and its multidisciplinary cancer meetings, held mostly weekly, include the specialist responsible for cancer surgery.
summary_en: Tyks says lung cancer diagnostics are centralised at its lung clinic and that its multidisciplinary cancer meetings, held mostly weekly, include the specialist responsible for cancer surgery. Varsinais-Suomi therefore already has a surgeon in the meeting, and our model counts this measure only in counties without a university hospital. The English evidence (Lau et al. 2013) points the same way, with resection rates of 20.0% where surgeons were based against 11.6% in peripheral hospitals, but it is observational.
unanswered_en: No page names a thoracic surgeon specifically in the lung cancer meeting; the Tyks page describes cancer meetings in general.
